item.text: I’m verifying the precedence order for merge sequences. The constructor behavior there is easy to get subtly wrong, and Python’s result is what matters.
I’m narrowing float formatting as well. If PyYAML normalizes decimals in a predictable way, I can keep that in one formatter instead of preserving original float text.
The float resolver is definitely not just “anything JavaScript can parse.” I’m checking exponent forms so I can mirror PyYAML’s narrower rules instead of guessing.
I’ve narrowed float resolution further: exponent notation is only being recognized in a subset of decimal forms. I’m checking the exact accepted variant and then I can codify it.
I’m checking one sexagesimal number case because YAML 1.1 supports it. If PyYAML still resolves it here, I’ll add a small handler; otherwise I can keep the resolver simpler.

I’m borrowing the block-header decision rules from a YAML dumper rather than inventing them, especially for cases like leading spaces that require an indentation indicator such as `>2-`.
I’m checking the start-with-newline case because that also affects whether the folded block needs an indentation indicator.
I’m checking trailing newlines now, because the block chomping indicator (`-`, empty, or `+`) is part of the exact output.
I’m checking one quoted-string fallback with an actual newline escape, so the double-quote escaper matches PyYAML if a string can’t be emitted as a folded block.

I have enough context to implement this cleanly. Plan:
1. Vendor the ESM YAML parser into `/output` as local `.mjs` modules.
2. Build a PyYAML-like loader on top of the AST so scalar resolution, merges, aliases, and Python dict key behavior match `safe_load`.

4. Add the manual argparse-compatible CLI in `test15.mjs` and verify it against the executable on the sample and edge cases.

item.text: I’m checking explicit numeric tags as well. PyYAML’s explicit constructors can be broader than its implicit plain-scalar resolver, and I don’t want to apply the wrong rule there.
I’m checking whether PyYAML’s `...` end marker for `>+` only appears at the document level or also when the kept-newline scalar is nested. That affects how the serializer threads this state upward.
I’m checking how multiple consecutive newlines collapse into folded-block paragraphs, so the emitter can handle more than just the single- and double-newline cases.
I found one important inconsistency: the same visible string can dump differently depending on whether it retains a trailing newline. I’m isolating that before finalizing the folded-string rules.
The previous “quoted multiline string” case was a false lead: YAML folded the physical line break during parsing. I’m now testing a true newline character inside the string using `\\n` escape syntax.
Actual newline strings line up with folded-style emission after all. The remaining string question is just word-wrapping for long single lines, so I’m comparing that behavior next.
